Where does a Treasury auction go?

When primary dealers take a large share of a ten-year note auction, how much does their net position change by settlement? Follow the weekly figures, then compare them with evidence on how quickly dealers sell individual bonds.

How long did dealers hold the bonds?

A dealer can sell a note before settlement, hold it for later resale or finance a customer who buys it. The auction result measures the par value awarded to dealers. Weekly reports measure the net position that remains after their other trades. Following the same note through a reopening helps distinguish these quantities.

In the 20 November 2026 snapshot, the median position change from before auction to the settlement report was +$0.36bn for high awards and +$0.57bn for low awards. One week later those medians were +$0.20bn and +$1.66bn. In this sample the high-award group recorded the smaller median increase at both horizons.

The Federal Reserve Board followed individual securities more closely using when-issued trades and regulatory TRACE records. For original issues from March 2016 to July 2025, its ten-year estimate put the time for post-auction inventory to fall by half at under half a day. Dealers could therefore have sold much of an award before the first weekly observation. The Board also found that financing provided to customers could persist after dealers had sold the securities. Definitions, timing and coverage

Compare award shares within the same reporting period and issue type. A reopening adds to a note already trading under the same CUSIP. A new issue introduces a new CUSIP. The group labels use historical awards and can only be assigned with the benefit of the full sample.

The matched series begins in April 2013, when the seven-to-eleven-year reporting bucket became available. The November 2026 vintage covers 164 regular auctions, 55 new issues and 109 reopenings. The first post-settlement observation is available for 163 auctions. The June 2019 contingency test is excluded.

Each maturity-bucket observation measures long positions less short positions at market value. For each horizon, the chart takes the median event-by-event change among the auctions with both endpoint reports. Later readings stop at reporting-period changes and at the next regular ten-year auction. Only 40 auctions have an eligible observation three weeks after the settlement report. The chart spaces its observation labels evenly; the number of days between auction and settlement varies.

Historical award-share thresholds by issue type and reporting period. Shares at or below the lower threshold enter the low group and shares at or above the upper threshold enter the high group. Thresholds shown to two decimal places.
Reporting periodIssue typeAuctionsLower thresholdUpper threshold

The baseline selector isolates two different intervals. The last report strictly before the auction includes subsequent when-issued trading in the measured change. The last report strictly before the issue date can already reflect the award and some trading. Settlement is represented by the first report on or after the issue date, which can fall several days later. The following observations are spaced a week apart.

Changes in this net position also reflect client orders, outright trades in other issues, changes in security prices and bonds moving across maturity buckets. Individual bonds can change hands several times between two reports. Establishing sales by CUSIP, the financing associated with those trades, or their effect on long yields requires additional observations.
